This guarded lookup avoids extrapolating path choices into traffic regions not supported by offline measurements. 4 Experiments We evaluate RailWave against Native, NCCL, and the released FAST implementation ( Lei et al., 2026 ) , isolate the effects of spatial and temporal shaping, and evaluate adaptive execution. Additional results on integration with an upper-layer expert-parallel system are provided in Appendix A.2 . 4.1 Experimental Setup Platforms. We evaluate on two 32-GPU clusters equipped with NVIDIA H800 and H20 GPUs, respectively. Each cluster has four nodes with eight GPUs per node. All compared methods use the same communication configuration within each cluster. Detailed hardware and software settings are provided in Appendix A.1 . Workloads. Our replay is based on expert-routing statistics collected during actual GLM-4.5-Air ( GLM-4.5 Team, 2025 ) training runs on DAPO-Math-17k ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , covering all 45 MoE layers. To model incast under variable rank progress, we construct three controlled sending patterns—Ring, Moderate, and Extreme—as detailed in Appendix A.6 . Baselines and metrics. We compare four execution paths on the same DeepEP backend: Native , Rail-only , Permutation-only , and Joint . Native and Rail-only retain the replayed transfer order, whereas Permutation-only and Joint use cyclic waves; Joint additionally applies RailBalance within each wave. RailWave selects among these paths using the calibrated lookup described in Section 3.3 . We also compare against NCCL all_to_all_single and the released FAST implementation. The plotted latency is the GPU-event communication interval: all waves of dispatch–combine for the DeepEP paths, or the corresponding forward–return All-to-All for NCCL and FAST, including RailBalance GPU operations when enabled. CPU planning, index construction, and prepacking are outside this interval for every method, as detailed in Appendix A.6 . Each plotted P50/P95/P99 is the sum of the corresponding per-layer quantiles over the 45-layer replay. 4.2 Overall Performance Communication performance. Figures 5 – 7 compare RailWave with Native, NCCL, and FAST under Ring, Moderate, and Extreme, respectively. RailWave achieves 2.02 2.02 – 5.84 × 5.84\times speedups over Native at P50 on H800 and 1.74 1.74 – 4.36 × 4.36\times on H20 across the three replay patterns, with gains persisting at P95 and P99. Native slows from Moderate to Extreme under stronger incast, whereas RailWave maintains nearly identical P50 latency across the two patterns. Figure 7 separates the contributions of RailBalance and permutation scheduling. In Ring, Rail-only closely matches Joint while Permutation-only remains close to Native, showing that spatial shaping provides most of the gain when incast is already limited. Under Moderate and Extreme, combining the two mechanisms improves performance on both clusters. On H800, Joint achieves 1.44 × 1.44\times and 1.97 × 1.97\times speedups over the better single mechanism, respectively. Figure 9 shows the effect of RailBalance under Moderate on H20. Native distributes transmitted traffic as approximately 54.12%, 24.33%, 14.85%, and 6.69% across the four NIC positions, whereas Rail-only and Joint produce approximately equal shares in both directions. Permutation-only retains the uneven distribution. These results show that RailBalance changes physical Rail utilization, whereas permutation scheduling changes which node-pair transfers overlap. Performance across replay-derived traffic conditions. We further select cases from the replay that span different levels of Rail skew and receiver concentration. Figure 9 shows that when both are high, Joint outperforms either single mechanism. In one such case, Joint reduces mean latency to 4.11 ms, compared with 10.96 ms for Permutation-only and 73.28 ms for Rail-only. More balanced cases can instead favor a lighter execution path, motivating adaptive selection. Adaptive execution. We evaluate the calibrated selector on 12 unseen requests that are not used to construct the frozen cost table. Figure 10 shows the four requests where the selector switches away from Joint: three select Permutation-only and one selects Native. All four switches reduce measured median communication latency, by 5.7–16.4%, corresponding to 1.061 1.061 – 1.196 × 1.196\times speedup over Joint. The remaining eight requests fall back to Joint. Additional UltraEP integration results, packing measurements, and workspace accounting are provided in Appendices A.2 , A.4 , and A.5 , respectively. 5 Conclusion We presented RailWave, a communication layer for expert-parallel MoE execution that targets physical-network inefficiencies remaining after expert routing and placement are fixed. RailWave combines source-local RailBalance with reusable permutation scheduling to jointly improve parallel Rail utilization and control receiver-side concurrency, while preserving expert assignments and logical communication demand. Built on DeepEP, RailWave achieves communication speedups of up to 5.84 × 5.84\times on H800 and 4.36 × 4.36\times on H20, demonstrating the benefits of jointly shaping the spatial and temporal execution of expert-parallel traffic.
